text: A nonrepeatable read happens when your transaction reads the same row twice and gets two different values -- because another transaction committed an update to that row in between your two reads. Unlike a dirty read, the value you saw the second time is completely real and committed.
Session A opens a transaction and reads a product's price. It gets back 34.99. That transaction is still open -- it hasn't committed or rolled back yet.

Session B, meanwhile, updates that same row's price to 49.99, and that update commits immediately under ordinary autocommit. This is a completely real, completely legitimate change -- not a dirty, in-flight value like last lesson.

Session A reads the same row again, still inside its original, still-open transaction. This time it gets 49.99 -- a different value than the first read. Session A asked the identical question twice within one logical unit of work and got two different answers. That's the nonrepeatable read.

READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED both allow this -- READ COMMITTED releases its shared locks as soon as each statement's read finishes, leaving a gap for Session B's update to slip through. REPEATABLE READ closes that gap: it holds a shared lock on every row it reads until its own transaction ends, which would have forced Session B's UPDATE to wait.

So nonrepeatable reads are allowed under READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, and prevented from REPEATABLE READ up. Next lesson, the third and final classic anomaly: the phantom read, where it's not a value that changes, but the whole set of rows a query returns. See you there.
